## Best e-commerce platforms for starting an online store

| Platform | Best for | Main strengths | Main drawbacks |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Shopify** | Most new businesses | Easiest all-in-one setup, strong checkout, payments, inventory, multichannel selling, and a large app ecosystem | Monthly fee plus possible app and transaction costs |
| **WooCommerce** | Maximum control and customization | Free, open-source WordPress plugin with extensive themes, extensions, and payment options | You manage hosting, security, updates, backups, and extensions |
| **BigCommerce** | Growing or complex stores | Strong built-in catalog, promotions, multi-channel, B2B, and international features | More expensive and potentially complex for a very small store |
| **Wix eCommerce** | Beginners who prioritize design | Easy drag-and-drop website building with integrated store features | Less suited to complex inventory, operations, or advanced analytics |
| **Squarespace Commerce** | Design-led brands and creators | Excellent templates and content/brand presentation | Less extensive e-commerce functionality than Shopify or BigCommerce |
| **Etsy** | Handmade, vintage, craft, and creative products | Built-in marketplace traffic and easy setup | You do not fully own the customer relationship; listing and transaction fees apply |

### My recommendations

**Choose Shopify for most first-time store owners.**  
It offers the best balance of ease, scalability, payments, shipping, inventory, and integrations. Shopify’s U.S. Basic plan is currently listed at **$39/month monthly or $29/month when billed annually**, with online selling, unlimited products, social/marketplace selling, and in-person selling included. ([shopify.com](https://www.shopify.com/pricing?utm_source=openai))

**Choose WooCommerce if you already use WordPress or need deep customization.**  
WooCommerce itself is free and open source, with no platform fee or revenue share, but you must budget separately for hosting, payment processing, themes, extensions, maintenance, and security. ([woocommerce.com](https://woocommerce.com/?locale=en&utm_source=openai))

**Choose BigCommerce if you expect substantial growth or need B2B features.**  
It has strong native commerce functionality and plans based partly on sales volume. Current self-serve pricing starts at **$39/month monthly or $29/month annually**, with automatic upgrades as sales exceed plan thresholds. ([bigcommerce.com](https://www.bigcommerce.com/pricing/?utm_source=openai))

**Choose Wix or Squarespace if your store is relatively simple and visual presentation matters most.**  
They are especially appropriate for artists, consultants, restaurants, fashion brands, and small catalogs where the website and brand experience are as important as the store itself. Wix provides integrated store features, while Squarespace emphasizes design and built-in commerce tools. ([wix.com](https://www.wix.com/plans?8c8410c7_page=1&b60bd69c_page=2&utm_source=openai))

**Choose Etsy as a sales channel—not necessarily as your only long-term home.**  
It can be a good way to test handmade or creative products because shoppers already visit the marketplace. However, Etsy charges listing and transaction fees; in the U.S., its standard fees include **$0.20 per listing** and a **6.5% transaction fee**, in addition to payment processing and possible advertising fees. ([etsy.com](https://www.etsy.com/sell?utm_source=openai))

## Simple decision rule

- **Want the easiest path?** Shopify  
- **Already use WordPress or want full control?** WooCommerce  
- **Selling B2B, internationally, or at larger volume?** BigCommerce  
- **Want a beautiful small-business website?** Wix or Squarespace  
- **Selling handmade or vintage goods?** Etsy plus your own Shopify/WooCommerce site  
- **Selling locally or in person too?** Shopify, especially if you want integrated POS  

For most people starting from scratch, I’d begin with **Shopify**, unless you already have a WordPress site or have unusual customization requirements.

For most growing online businesses, **Shopify is the best default choice**: it’s hosted, relatively easy to operate, has a large app ecosystem, and scales from a small store to enterprise through Shopify Plus. Current U.S. pricing starts at **$39/month monthly or $29/month annually** for Basic; Grow is $105/$79, and Advanced is $399/$299. ([shopify.com](https://www.shopify.com/pricing?utm_source=openai))

## Best options by situation

| Platform | Best for | Main advantage | Main drawback |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Shopify** | Most DTC/B2C brands | Easiest all-around scaling, strong checkout, hosting and security included | Apps and transaction fees can raise total cost |
| **BigCommerce** | Larger catalogs, B2B, multichannel selling | Strong built-in commerce features and broad payment-provider support | Pricing and payment-provider fees require careful review |
| **WooCommerce** | WordPress businesses and highly customized stores | Flexible, open-source, no platform revenue share | You manage hosting, updates, security, and more technical work |
| **Adobe Commerce** | Large enterprises with complex B2B/multibrand needs | Deep customization and enterprise functionality | Usually expensive and requires a development team |

### My recommendation

**Choose Shopify if:**
- You want to launch or improve quickly.
- Your team is small or nontechnical.
- You sell primarily direct-to-consumer.
- You need strong integrations for email, subscriptions, social selling, marketplaces, and retail POS.
- You prefer predictable hosting and security rather than managing infrastructure.

**Choose BigCommerce if:**
- You need advanced catalog, pricing, promotions, or B2B functionality without building everything through apps.
- You sell through multiple channels or use third-party payment providers.
- You expect substantial growth and want built-in features before relying heavily on extensions.

BigCommerce currently lists Core, Growth, and Scale plans at **$39, $105, and $399 per month** when billed monthly, with lower annual prices. Its 2026 pricing also adds fees for orders processed through certain “Open Payment Providers” on self-service plans, so payment processing should be modeled carefully before choosing it. ([bigcommerce.com](https://www.bigcommerce.com/pricing/?utm_source=openai))

**Choose WooCommerce if:**
- Your website is already built on WordPress.
- Content marketing, SEO, and editorial flexibility are central.
- You have technical support or are comfortable managing hosting and plugins.
- You want more control over data, checkout, and customization.

WooCommerce itself is free and has no platform revenue share, but you pay separately for hosting, payment processing, extensions, maintenance, and development. WooCommerce estimates hosting for most stores at roughly **$25–$350/month**, depending on requirements. ([woocommerce.com](https://woocommerce.com/pricing/?trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block&utm_source=openai))

**Choose Adobe Commerce only if:**
- You have complex B2B workflows, multiple brands, regions, catalogs, or customer-specific pricing.
- You have an established engineering or agency budget.
- Your needs exceed what Shopify or BigCommerce can support without extensive customization.

Adobe offers Commerce as cloud-based SaaS or dedicated cloud infrastructure, but pricing is quote-based rather than publicly listed. ([business.adobe.com](https://business.adobe.com/products/commerce/pricing.html?b60bd69c_page=1&utm_source=openai))

## Bottom line

- **Best overall:** Shopify  
- **Best for feature-rich scaling and B2B:** BigCommerce  
- **Best for WordPress and maximum control:** WooCommerce  
- **Best for complex enterprise commerce:** Adobe Commerce  

Before committing, compare **total cost**, not just the monthly subscription: payment-processing rates, third-party transaction fees, apps/extensions, shipping, tax tools, email/SMS, development, and migration costs can matter more than the base plan.

The **best open-source e-commerce platform depends on your store’s complexity, technical team, and willingness to manage hosting and updates**. My current shortlist is:

| Platform | Best for | Main advantages | Main drawbacks |
|---|---|---|---|
| **WooCommerce** | Small to midsize stores already using WordPress | Easiest entry point, huge WordPress ecosystem, highly customizable, free/open-source core | Plugin conflicts, maintenance burden, and performance can suffer with poorly chosen extensions |
| **PrestaShop** | Traditional, international small-to-midsize stores | Dedicated commerce platform, multilingual and multicurrency capabilities, strong catalog and back-office features | Add-ons can become expensive; requires more technical administration than WooCommerce |
| **Shopware Community Edition** | Growing European and mid-market merchants | Modern admin, sales channels, promotions, rules, multilingual support, APIs, and good built-in commerce functionality | More complex than WooCommerce; some advanced capabilities are commercial |
| **Magento Open Source** | Large catalogs, complex pricing, multi-store, and enterprise-style operations | Very powerful catalog, inventory, customer, store-view, and extension capabilities | High hosting, development, security, and maintenance costs; usually overkill for smaller stores |
| **Saleor** | Developer-led, headless, global commerce projects | GraphQL/API-first architecture, composable design, extensible dashboard, strong international and omnichannel potential | Requires a capable engineering team and a separately built or customized frontend |
| **Medusa** | Custom JavaScript/Node.js commerce applications | Flexible modular architecture, headless storefronts, custom workflows, marketplaces, subscriptions, and complex B2C use cases | More of a developer platform than a ready-to-launch merchant solution |
| **Sylius** | Bespoke B2B, B2C, and mid-market commerce | Symfony-based, modular, API-first, highly customizable, and well suited to custom business rules | Requires PHP/Symfony expertise and generally needs agency or in-house development |

### My practical recommendations

- **Best overall for most small businesses:** **WooCommerce**  
  Choose it if you already use WordPress, need content marketing, and want the broadest selection of themes and extensions. WooCommerce’s core is free and open source, with no monthly platform fee. ([woocommerce.com](https://woocommerce.com/woocommerce/?utm_source=openai))

- **Best dedicated alternative to WooCommerce:** **PrestaShop**  
  It is a better fit when the store itself—not a content site—is the center of the business, especially for multiple languages, countries, currencies, and tax environments. PrestaShop 9 uses Symfony 6.4, PHP 8.1+, and includes an Admin API. ([prestashop.com](https://prestashop.com/open-source/?utm_source=openai))

- **Best for a polished mid-market platform:** **Shopware Community Edition**  
  Shopware provides built-in sales channels, customer groups, promotions, rule-based pricing, SEO, flows, APIs, and multilingual/currency support. ([shopware.com](https://www.shopware.com/en/community/community-edition/?utm_source=openai))

- **Best for complex or enterprise catalogs:** **Magento Open Source**  
  Use it when you genuinely need complex catalogs, multiple websites/stores, custom pricing, or sophisticated integrations—and have an experienced technical team. Adobe maintains release notes for Magento Open Source, but Adobe explicitly treats it as separate from Adobe Commerce and does not provide the same support or commercial feature set. ([experienceleague.adobe.com](https://experienceleague.adobe.com/en/docs/commerce-operations/release/notes/magento-open-source/overview?utm_source=openai))

- **Best modern headless option:** **Saleor**  
  Saleor is a strong choice for teams building custom web, mobile, retail, or omnichannel experiences around a GraphQL API. Its dashboard includes product-information and order-management capabilities, but frontend and integration work remain significant. ([saleor.io](https://saleor.io/?utm_source=openai))

- **Best for custom Node.js commerce:** **Medusa**  
  Medusa is particularly suitable for unusual B2C workflows, subscriptions, marketplaces, custom checkout, multiple regions, and integrations with external systems. ([medusajs.com](https://medusajs.com/b2c?utm_source=openai))

- **Best for custom Symfony/PHP implementations:** **Sylius**  
  Sylius is better viewed as a highly customizable commerce framework than a plug-and-play store builder. It supports API-driven projects, custom checkout and order flows, multiple currencies, and integrations with PIM, CRM, and marketing systems. ([sylius.com](https://sylius.com/about/?utm_source=openai))

### Simple decision guide

- **Launching quickly with a modest budget:** WooCommerce or PrestaShop  
- **WordPress content site plus store:** WooCommerce  
- **International store with built-in commerce tools:** PrestaShop or Shopware  
- **Large catalog or complicated multi-store setup:** Magento Open Source or Shopware  
- **Custom React/Next.js/mobile storefront:** Saleor or Medusa  
- **Highly specialized B2B workflows:** Sylius, Medusa, or Magento  
- **Small store with minimal technical resources:** WooCommerce—ideally with managed hosting—or consider a hosted platform instead of self-hosting

One important caveat: **“open source” does not mean zero-cost**. You still pay for hosting, payment processing, backups, security, updates, development, extensions, monitoring, and often professional support. For most businesses, the best platform is the one their team can reliably maintain—not necessarily the one with the most features.

For your situation, I’d start with **Square Online**.

Because you already sell at local markets, Square lets you manage **in-person sales and online orders from the same product catalog and inventory system**. Its free online plan includes a basic store, shipping, local delivery, pickup, customer accounts, and social selling. You pay processing fees when you make a sale rather than a monthly subscription. ([squareup.com](https://squareup.com/us/en/online-store/plans?msockid=1bc36084ea7b6f62259276d6eb156e3d&utm_source=openai))

## Best options

### 1. **Square Online — best starting point**
Choose this if you want:

- Low upfront cost
- Local pickup and shipping
- Inventory shared with your market booth
- A Square card reader for in-person events
- A simple store you can launch quickly

The free plan currently charges **2.9% + $0.30 per online transaction**. Square Plus is listed at **$29/month when billed annually** and adds more customization, subscriptions, scheduled product drops, and a custom domain. ([squareup.com](https://squareup.com/us/en/online-store/plans?msockid=1bc36084ea7b6f62259276d6eb156e3d&utm_source=openai))

**My recommendation:** Start with Square Free, then upgrade only if you need a more polished branded site.

### 2. **Shopify — best for serious growth**
Choose Shopify if you expect to build a larger brand with:

- Many candle scents and seasonal collections
- Subscriptions or candle-of-the-month clubs
- More advanced marketing and analytics
- Multiple sales channels
- More control over your storefront

Shopify’s Basic plan is listed at **$29/month when billed annually**, or **$39 month-to-month**, with online card rates starting at **2.9% + $0.30**. It also supports in-person selling through Shopify POS. ([shopify.com](https://www.shopify.com/pricing?utm_source=openai))

It is more powerful than you probably need at first, but it may be worth choosing if you already have strong demand and want a long-term ecommerce platform.

### 3. **Etsy — useful as an additional sales channel**
Etsy can help you reach people already searching for handmade candles, but I would not make it your only online presence. Etsy charges a **$0.20 listing fee**, a **6.5% transaction fee**, payment-processing fees, and potentially offsite-ad fees. ([etsy.com](https://www.etsy.com/sell?utm_source=openai))

A good approach is:

- **Square or Shopify** = your own branded store and customer list
- **Etsy** = an additional place for discovery and new customers

## What I would do in your shoes

1. Create a **Square Online** store.
2. Use your own domain, such as `yourcandlename.com`.
3. Start with 10–20 best-selling products rather than listing everything.
4. Offer:
   - Shipping
   - Local pickup
   - “Pick up at the next market” if practical
5. Add a QR code to your booth that links directly to your store.
6. Collect email addresses with customer permission.
7. Photograph each candle consistently and include scent notes, size, burn time, ingredients, and safety instructions.
8. Review sales after two or three months. Move to Shopify only if you need more advanced features.

**Bottom line:** Start with **Square Online** for simplicity and low cost. Add **Etsy** for discovery, and consider **Shopify** later if your candle business grows into a larger online brand.

**My default recommendation: migrate to Shopify—Shopify Plus if you’re doing serious holiday volume.**

Your two symptoms—**traffic-related crashes** and **plugin conflicts**—usually point toward reducing self-hosted infrastructure and third-party code. Shopify Plus provides managed hosting, CDN-backed infrastructure, automatic updates, DDoS protection, and enterprise support, which removes much of the server and plugin-maintenance burden. ([help.shopify.com](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/intro-to-shopify/pricing-plans/plans-features/shopify-plus-plan?utm_source=openai))

### Choose Shopify Plus if you want

- The lowest operational burden
- Reliable performance during traffic spikes
- A large app ecosystem, but with more controlled checkout extensions
- Strong hosted checkout and payment infrastructure
- Multiple stores, international selling, B2B/D2C, or enterprise integrations
- A team that would rather configure commerce than maintain servers

Shopify’s current checkout-extensibility model is app-based and designed to be upgrade-safe, replacing older direct-code approaches such as `checkout.liquid`. That should reduce the kind of conflicts you’re experiencing—but you’ll still need to audit apps carefully. ([help.shopify.com](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/checkout-settings/customize-checkout-configurations/checkout-extensibility?utm_source=openai))

### Choose BigCommerce instead if you need more built-in flexibility

BigCommerce is probably the better choice if your store has:

- Complex catalogs or pricing rules
- B2B accounts, quoting, or customer-specific price lists
- Heavy ERP, PIM, OMS, or marketplace integrations
- A headless storefront
- A desire to avoid excessive platform lock-in
- A development team that wants broad API access and more control

It is a fully hosted platform with enterprise scalability, API-first architecture, B2B functionality, and a reported 99.99% uptime target. ([bigcommerce.com](https://www.bigcommerce.com/articles/ecommerce/enterprise-ecommerce-platforms/?utm_source=openai))

### I would not choose another plugin-heavy setup

I would **not** move from WooCommerce to another self-hosted WordPress/WooCommerce implementation merely to solve this problem. WooCommerce can scale, but its own documentation acknowledges that performance depends heavily on hosting, themes, and other plugins; enterprise deployments generally require staging, version control, backups, and dedicated optimization work. ([woocommerce.com](https://woocommerce.com/document/woocommerce-scaling-faqs/?utm_source=openai))

### Practical decision

| Situation | Best fit |
|---|---|
| You want stability and minimal maintenance | **Shopify** |
| High-volume holiday sales or enterprise operations | **Shopify Plus** |
| Complex B2B, catalog, pricing, or ERP requirements | **BigCommerce Enterprise** |
| Highly customized commerce with a large engineering team | BigCommerce or Adobe Commerce |
| Small-to-mid-sized store with moderate traffic | Shopify standard plans |

**Bottom line:** Unless you have unusually complex B2B or integration requirements, I’d migrate to **Shopify Plus**, aggressively limit the app count, and replace custom plugin logic with native features, Shopify Functions, Flow, and supported app extensions.

Before signing, run a migration proof of concept covering your top 20 products, customer accounts, historical orders, promotions, subscriptions, tax/shipping rules, analytics, and every checkout path. Also load-test the exact holiday campaign—not just the homepage.

For a **B2B wholesaler with thousands of products**, my default shortlist would be:

1. **BigCommerce B2B Edition** — best general-purpose choice for many mid-market wholesalers  
2. **Sana Commerce Cloud** — best if your business runs on Microsoft Dynamics or SAP  
3. **OroCommerce** — best for highly complex wholesale pricing, accounts, workflows, and quoting  
4. **Adobe Commerce** — best for large, technically sophisticated organizations needing deep customization  
5. **Shopify Plus** — best when B2B and DTC need to coexist and the B2B model is relatively straightforward

## My default recommendation: BigCommerce B2B Edition

I would start with **BigCommerce B2B Edition** unless your ERP or pricing model points strongly toward another platform. It provides company accounts, buyer roles and permissions, account hierarchies, price lists, sales-rep quoting, bulk ordering, and B2B buyer portals. Those are the capabilities a wholesaler usually needs without requiring a heavily custom commerce implementation. ([support.bigcommerce.com](https://support.bigcommerce.com/s/article/B2B-Edition?language=en_US&r=358&utm_source=openai))

It is particularly suitable if you need:

- Thousands or tens of thousands of SKUs
- Customer-specific price lists
- Multiple buyers per customer account
- Quick order by SKU or CSV
- Reordering and order history
- Sales-rep-assisted orders and quotes
- ERP, CRM, PIM, and fulfillment integrations
- A managed SaaS platform rather than maintaining servers

## Choose Sana if your ERP is the source of truth

If you use **Microsoft Dynamics or SAP**, strongly consider **Sana Commerce Cloud**. Sana is designed to read products, customers, inventory, prices, discounts, payment terms, and customer-specific pricing directly from the ERP rather than maintaining a separate ecommerce database. That can substantially reduce synchronization problems for wholesalers with complicated pricing and inventory rules. ([sana-commerce.com](https://www.sana-commerce.com/pricing/?utm_source=openai))

Sana is especially attractive when:

- Your ERP already contains the authoritative customer and product data
- Pricing differs by customer, contract, quantity, or discount group
- Real-time inventory and order status are important
- You want to avoid middleware and duplicate data
- You use SAP, Dynamics 365, Business Central, NAV, or related systems

## Choose OroCommerce for complex B2B operations

**OroCommerce** is a strong fit for distributors and wholesalers with unusually complex business rules. It supports corporate account hierarchies, customer-specific catalogs and pricing, RFQs, quick orders, reorders, workflows, multiple warehouses, customer part numbers, and complex quote-to-order processes. ([oroinc.com](https://oroinc.com/b2b-ecommerce/orocommerce-features/?utm_source=openai))

Consider it if you need:

- Different catalogs and pricing for many accounts
- Parent/child companies and delegated purchasing
- Complex approval workflows
- Built-in quoting or CPQ
- Customer-specific SKUs or product cross-references
- Sales-rep tools and buyer impersonation
- A unified commerce, CRM, PIM, and workflow platform

The tradeoff is that it may require a more specialized implementation partner and a more deliberate evaluation than a mainstream SaaS platform.

## Choose Adobe Commerce for maximum customization

**Adobe Commerce** is appropriate when you need significant customization, multiple websites or brands, complex catalogs, extensive integrations, or a combined B2B/B2C operation. Its B2B capabilities include company accounts, shared catalogs, custom pricing, negotiable quotes, purchase orders, quick order, and requisition lists. ([experienceleague.adobe.com](https://experienceleague.adobe.com/en/docs/commerce-admin/b2b/introduction?utm_source=openai))

Choose it when:

- You have a capable internal IT or ecommerce team
- You need unusual catalog, pricing, or checkout logic
- You operate multiple brands, regions, or storefronts
- You need deep control over the architecture
- You are comfortable with a larger implementation and maintenance burden

For a typical wholesaler, Adobe Commerce can be more platform than necessary unless the business processes are genuinely complex.

## Choose Shopify Plus for simpler B2B plus DTC

- Its newer checkout extensibility model is designed to replace fragile theme edits, scripts, and direct checkout modifications with supported app extensions. ([help.shopify.com](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/checkout-settings/customize-checkout-configurations/checkout-extensibility?utm_source=openai))
- It has a large app ecosystem, but you should still reduce your app count and avoid installing multiple apps that control the same function—such as subscriptions, discounts, reviews, analytics, or cart upsells.

**Best for:** DTC retail, moderate-to-high traffic, small technical teams, quick migration, and predictable operations.

#### 2. **BigCommerce: better if you need more built-in flexibility**
Consider BigCommerce instead if you have substantial B2B requirements, complex catalogs, multiple price lists, purchase orders, or need more checkout control without going fully custom.

- BigCommerce provides a managed SaaS environment while offering no-code and full-code checkout customization. ([bigcommerce.com](https://www.bigcommerce.com/product/checkout/?utm_source=openai))
- It may let you replace more plugins with native catalog, pricing, promotion, and checkout features.

**Best for:** B2B, complex product/pricing rules, larger catalogs, and merchants who want a more open platform without managing servers.

#### 3. **Avoid WooCommerce for this particular problem**
WooCommerce can work well, but it is unlikely to solve your underlying issues by itself. It remains dependent on WordPress hosting, themes, caching, database tuning, and extension compatibility. WooCommerce’s own documentation emphasizes caching, image optimization, database maintenance, CDNs, and extension compatibility as ongoing performance concerns. ([developer.woocommerce.com](https://developer.woocommerce.com/docs/extensions/getting-started-extensions/?utm_source=openai))

#### 4. **Use Adobe Commerce only if you have enterprise-level complexity**
Adobe Commerce can scale and now supports cloud auto-scaling and more isolated, out-of-process extensions. ([experienceleague.adobe.com](https://experienceleague.adobe.com/en/docs/commerce-on-cloud/user-guide/architecture/autoscaling?utm_source=openai)) But it requires a serious engineering, QA, and operations budget. It is not the best choice merely because your current WordPress/WooCommerce setup is unstable.

### Practical decision

| Your situation | Pick |
|---|---|
| You want reliability and minimal maintenance | **Shopify** |
| You need advanced B2B/catalog/checkout flexibility | **BigCommerce** |
| You have a strong WordPress team and want maximum control | WooCommerce, but fix the architecture |
| You have enterprise integrations and dedicated engineers | Adobe Commerce |

### Important: do not recreate the plugin problem

During migration, aim for:

1. **Native platform features first**
2. **One app per business function**
3. **API/webhook integrations instead of theme hacks**
4. **A staging store and load test before November**
5. **A freeze on new apps before the holiday campaign**
6. **Monitoring for checkout errors, inventory sync, payment failures, and webhooks**

If your store is primarily DTC, I would choose **Shopify**. If it is B2B-heavy or depends on complex pricing and checkout workflows, I would choose **BigCommerce**.

For a **B2B wholesaler with thousands of products**, my default recommendation would be:

## Best overall starting point: **BigCommerce B2B Edition**

It is usually the strongest balance of B2B functionality, scalability, and implementation effort. It supports:

- Company accounts and account hierarchies
- Buyer roles and permissions
- Customer-specific price lists
- Quotes and sales-rep-assisted ordering
- Purchase approvals
- Quick ordering by SKU and CSV upload
- Shopping lists and reordering
- Invoices and payment management
- Multi-storefront support
- ERP/PIM integrations and headless options ([support.bigcommerce.com](https://support.bigcommerce.com/s/article/B2B-Edition-User-Guide?language=en_US&utm_source=openai))

It is a good fit if you want a serious wholesale portal without taking on as much infrastructure and customization as Adobe Commerce.

## Shortlist by business complexity

| Situation | Best candidates | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Mid-market wholesaler wanting a manageable SaaS platform | **BigCommerce B2B Edition** | Strong native B2B tools, bulk ordering, pricing, quotes, approvals, and company accounts |
| Complex pricing, customer-specific catalogs, subsidiaries, approvals, and heavy ERP integration | **Adobe Commerce B2B** or **OroCommerce** | Deep account hierarchies, shared catalogs, negotiated quotes, purchase orders, requisition lists, and customizable workflows |
| Mostly simple wholesale ordering, with a strong DTC brand or Shopify expertise | **Shopify Plus** | Easier administration and excellent general commerce ecosystem; better when B2B rules are relatively straightforward |
| Very complex manufacturing/distribution processes or highly customized workflows | **OroCommerce** | Built specifically around B2B account structures, price lists, RFQs, workflows, sales tools, and distributor use cases |
| Large enterprise already invested in Salesforce | **Salesforce B2B Commerce** | Makes more sense when Salesforce CRM, Sales Cloud, and enterprise identity infrastructure are already central |

### When to choose Adobe Commerce

Choose **Adobe Commerce** if your requirements include many customer-specific assortments and prices, complex company structures, purchase-order approvals, negotiated quotes, quick order, and recurring requisition lists. Its B2B features include company hierarchies, shared catalogs, custom pricing, quotes, purchase-on-account, purchase-order approvals, quick order, and requisition lists. ([experienceleague.adobe.com](https://experienceleague.adobe.com/en/docs/commerce-admin/b2b/introduction?utm_source=openai))

The tradeoff is that implementation, hosting, upgrades, and customization are generally more demanding than with a SaaS platform.

### When to choose OroCommerce

Choose **OroCommerce** if you are a distributor or wholesaler with unusually complex pricing and selling processes. It is designed around multiple catalogs, customer-specific price lists, RFQs, workflows, buyer hierarchies, inventory visibility, customer part numbers, bulk ordering, and ERP integration. ([oroinc.com](https://oroinc.com/b2b-ecommerce/orocommerce-features/?utm_source=openai))

It is especially worth evaluating if you need to digitize sales-rep processes—not just put a product catalog online.

### When Shopify Plus is enough

Shopify is appropriate if your wholesale model is relatively simple: a few catalogs, limited approval logic, standard payment terms, and modest quoting requirements. Shopify now includes native B2B features such as company profiles, catalogs, volume pricing, quantity rules, payment terms, and vaulted payment methods; Plus adds more extensive catalogs and company/location assignment. ([shopify.com](https://www.shopify.com/news/b2b-for-all?utm_source=openai))

I would not make it the first choice if your business depends heavily on intricate contract pricing, multiple buyer roles, negotiated quotes, account credit, or complex ERP-driven availability.

## What matters more than the number of SKUs

“Thousands of products” is not, by itself, a difficult requirement. Evaluate these instead:

1. **Pricing complexity** — one price per customer, tier pricing, contract pricing, promotions, rebates?
2. **Catalog visibility** — does each customer see a different assortment?
3. **Ordering method** — browsing, SKU entry, CSV upload, EDI, punchout, saved lists?
4. **Account structure** — multiple buyers, branches, subsidiaries, approval limits?
5. **Sales workflow** — quotes, RFQs, sales-rep ordering, negotiated freight?
6. **Inventory source** — ERP, WMS, multiple warehouses, real-time availability?
7. **Payment terms** — credit limits, invoices, ACH, purchase orders?
8. **Product data** — do you need a dedicated PIM for specifications, documents, compatibility, and technical attributes?
9. **Integration quality** — can the platform reliably sync customers, products, prices, inventory, orders, and invoices with your ERP?

## My practical recommendation

- **Choose BigCommerce B2B Edition** for the best general-purpose starting point.
- **Choose OroCommerce** if your business is genuinely B2B-first and pricing/workflows are complex.
- **Choose Adobe Commerce** if you need maximum flexibility and have the budget and technical team to manage it.
- **Choose Shopify Plus** only if ease of use and DTC capability matter more than deep wholesale complexity.

Before selecting one, require each vendor to demonstrate your actual scenarios using real sample data:

- Import 10,000–100,000 products
- Show three customers with different catalogs and prices
- Place a bulk order by SKU/CSV
- Apply customer-specific pricing and quantity breaks
- Route an order through buyer approval
- Create and convert a quote
- Display live inventory from your ERP
- Show invoices, credit limits, and order history
- Demonstrate search for manufacturer part numbers and customer-specific SKUs

That test will reveal much more than a generic product demo.

| **Saleor** | High-growth, international, headless commerce | GraphQL/API-first, multi-channel, multi-currency, multi-language, strong catalog and order capabilities | More complex deployment and frontend development |
| **Sylius** | Custom B2B/B2C systems built with PHP/Symfony | Excellent framework for bespoke business rules, clean architecture, flexible APIs | Best suited to experienced Symfony/PHP teams rather than beginners |

### Choose **WooCommerce** if…
You already use WordPress, need to launch quickly, or want the broadest selection of themes, extensions, payment gateways, and freelancers. ### Choose **Medusa** if…
You have developers and want a custom storefront, marketplace, subscription workflow, or unusual checkout and fulfillment logic. Medusa provides open-source commerce modules for products, inventory, carts, payments, orders, and related functionality, with a framework for extending the underlying business logic. ([docs.medusajs.com](https://docs.medusajs.com/learn?utm_source=openai))

### Choose **Saleor** if…
You are building a modern, international, API-first store with multiple channels or frontends. Saleor is headless and GraphQL-native, with support for multi-channel pricing, currencies, languages, warehouses, promotions, payments, and complex catalogs. ([github.com](https://github.com/saleor/saleor?utm_source=openai))

### Choose **Sylius** if…
Your commerce requirements are unique—for example, complex B2B pricing, custom ordering workflows, multiple sales channels, or unusual fulfillment rules—and your team is comfortable with Symfony. Sylius describes itself as an open-source e-commerce framework rather than a rigid turnkey store platform. ([github.com](https://github.com/sylius/sylius?utm_source=openai))

### Choose **Magento Open Source** if…
You need a serious multi-store, large-catalog system and can afford a professional development and operations team. Magento Open Source remains Adobe-supported and offers a substantial extension ecosystem, but it is usually overkill for a small store. ([business.adobe.com](https://business.adobe.com/products/commerce/magento.html?utm_source=openai))

### Choose **PrestaShop** if…
You want a conventional self-hosted store with strong multilingual and localization capabilities. ([prestashop-project.org](https://www.prestashop-project.org/about/?utm_source=openai))

### Choose **OpenCart** if…
You want a relatively lightweight, conventional shopping-cart platform and do not need the architectural flexibility of a headless framework. Its marketplace advertises more than 13,000 modules and themes. ([opencart.com](https://www.opencart.com/?utm_source=openai))

## Short answer

- **Best for most small businesses:** WooCommerce  
- **Best modern headless platform:** Saleor  
- **Best for JavaScript developers:** Medusa  
- **Best for custom PHP/Symfony projects:** Sylius  
- **Best for large, complex catalogs:** Magento Open Source  
- **Best traditional international store:** PrestaShop

You may still pay for hosting, backups, security, development, premium extensions, payment processing, and maintenance. - **Less plugin conflict risk:** Shopify apps can still conflict, but the platform validates certain app installation requirements and prevents incompatible apps from being installed in some cases. ([help.shopify.com](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/apps/finding-choosing-apps?utm_source=openai))

### Which plan?

- **Shopify standard/Advanced:** Best if you are a small-to-mid-sized store, have moderate traffic, and mainly need reliability without enterprise pricing.
- **Shopify Plus:** Best if outages during Black Friday/Cyber Monday materially hurt revenue, you run frequent launches, need multiple stores/markets, have complex B2B requirements, or require priority enterprise support. Shopify lists U.S. Plus pricing starting at **$2,500/month on a one-year term** for standard setups, with possible variable fees for more complex businesses. ([help.shopify.com](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/intro-to-shopify/pricing-plans/plans-features/shopify-plus-plan?utm_source=openai))

### Strong alternative: BigCommerce

Choose **BigCommerce** instead if you need more built-in catalog, pricing, international, or B2B flexibility and want to avoid relying heavily on apps. Its SaaS model handles platform maintenance, while its API and integration ecosystem are designed for connecting external systems. ([investors.bigcommerce.com](https://investors.bigcommerce.com/static-files/55e214f7-33da-46b1-a58d-d9f0839dbe3c?utm_source=openai))

### I would avoid migrating to another self-hosted WordPress/WooCommerce setup

That could improve hosting performance, but it probably would not solve the underlying operational problem. WooCommerce’s own documentation acknowledges that third-party extensions are not guaranteed to work together and recommends staging-based conflict testing. ([woocommerce.com](https://woocommerce.com/document/how-to-test-for-conflicts/?utm_source=openai)) WooCommerce can scale with excellent managed hosting, but you would still own much more of the plugin, theme, hosting, caching, and update compatibility burden. ([woocommerce.com](https://woocommerce.com/hosting-solutions/?utm_source=openai))

### Practical recommendation

1. **Shortlist Shopify and BigCommerce.**
2. Export your last 12 months of orders, customers, products, discounts, subscriptions, and SEO URLs.
3. Rebuild the top 20 customer journeys in a staging store.
4. Run a load test against a realistic holiday scenario.
5. Test payments, tax, shipping, returns, inventory syncing, email flows, subscriptions, and analytics.
6. Keep the current store live while running a parallel migration and redirect plan.
7. Freeze nonessential changes several weeks before your holiday peak.

**Bottom line:** Choose **Shopify** for the lowest operational burden and strongest default choice for seasonal traffic spikes. Choose **BigCommerce** if your catalog, B2B pricing, or integrations are unusually complex.

Your symptoms—holiday crashes and recurring plugin conflicts—usually indicate that you’re carrying too much operational responsibility in a self-hosted stack. - Managed hosting and a standardized checkout rather than maintaining WordPress, PHP, databases, caching, and plugin compatibility.
- Strong peak-season resilience. Shopify Plus advertises load-tested checkout capacity of more than 10,000 checkouts per minute, unlimited bandwidth and transactions, and support for very large catalogs. Treat those as Shopify’s published platform claims and validate them against your own traffic profile. ([shopify.com](https://www.shopify.com/plus?utm_source=openai))
- Fewer fragile integrations: replace many plugins with Shopify apps, native features, Shopify Functions, APIs, or webhooks.
- Safer seasonal testing: Shopify supports draft checkout configurations so you can test changes before high-traffic periods. ([help.shopify.com](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/checkout-settings/customize-checkout-configurations/active-and-draft-checkouts?utm_source=openai))

**Important caveat:** Shopify reduces infrastructure and plugin risk; it does not eliminate app conflicts. Also, deep checkout customizations now need to use Shopify’s checkout-extensibility model rather than legacy `checkout.liquid` customizations. ([help.shopify.com](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/checkout-settings/customize-checkout-configurations/checkout-extensibility?utm_source=openai))

### Choose BigCommerce instead if you need:

- More control over the checkout, catalog logic, or complex B2B workflows.
- A highly customized checkout without giving up SaaS hosting.
- A headless storefront or custom checkout built with APIs/SDKs. BigCommerce offers an open-source checkout, Checkout SDK, Storefront APIs, and custom-checkout options. ([docs.bigcommerce.com](https://docs.bigcommerce.com/developer/docs/admin/checkout-and-cart?utm_source=openai))

### I would not migrate to another WooCommerce setup

Unless you have a strong engineering team and a clear reason to retain WordPress, moving from one WooCommerce host to another may improve performance but won’t remove the underlying plugin/theme compatibility problem. WooCommerce remains dependent on your hosting, caching, database, and extension stack. ([woocommerce.com](https://woocommerce.com/document/how-to-test-for-conflicts/?utm_source=openai))

### Practical decision

- **Typical DTC store:** Shopify.
- **Large/high-volume store or multiple brands/markets:** Shopify Plus.
- **Complex B2B, custom pricing, unusual checkout, or headless requirements:** BigCommerce Enterprise.
- **Content-heavy WordPress business where commerce is secondary:** consider keeping WordPress as the CMS and using Shopify or BigCommerce for commerce.

For a holiday migration, I’d avoid launching immediately before **Black Friday on November 27, 2026**. Migrate the catalog and customer data first, run a parallel staging store, load-test the peak traffic and checkout flow, freeze nonessential changes, and cut over only after payment, tax, shipping, inventory, email, analytics, redirects, and refunds have all been tested.

## Short answer

For a B2B wholesaler with thousands of products, my **default recommendation is BigCommerce B2B Edition**—especially if you need customer-specific pricing, account hierarchies, sales-rep assistance, quick ordering, quotes, purchase orders, and ERP integration without building everything from scratch.

BigCommerce’s B2B tools include company accounts with multiple buyers and permissions, price lists, quotes, invoice/payment portals, shared shopping lists, buy-again ordering, SKU/CSV quick order, and company-specific payment terms. ([support.bigcommerce.com](https://support.bigcommerce.com/s/article/B2B-Edition?language=en_US&r=358&utm_source=openai))

### Best-fit shortlist

| Platform | Best for | Main caution |
|---|---|---|
| **BigCommerce B2B Edition** | Most mid-market wholesalers and distributors | Some advanced features require the B2B Edition/Enterprise tier |
| **Shopify Plus** | Wholesalers that also have a significant DTC brand and want fast implementation | Complex customer-specific catalogs and pricing can push you toward Plus and additional customization |
| **Adobe Commerce** | Complex catalogs, many websites, sophisticated pricing, custom workflows, and deep ERP integration | More expensive and technically demanding to implement and maintain |
| **OroCommerce** | Businesses wanting a purpose-built B2B platform with highly customized workflows | Smaller ecosystem and generally requires more specialized implementation |

## My recommendation by scenario

### Choose **BigCommerce B2B Edition** if:

- You sell to many businesses with different price lists.
- Customers have multiple buyers, locations, departments, or approval rules.
- Buyers need to reorder from past orders or upload SKU lists.
- Sales reps still place orders on behalf of customers.
- You need quotes, purchase orders, credit terms, and invoice history.
- You want a SaaS platform rather than managing your own infrastructure.

This is probably the strongest general-purpose choice for a traditional wholesaler.

### Choose **Shopify Plus** if:

- You have both wholesale and consumer sales.
- Brand experience, marketing, and speed of launch are major priorities.
- Your wholesale pricing is relatively standardized.
- You want a large app and agency ecosystem.
- Your ERP/PIM can handle much of the complex pricing and product logic.

Shopify now provides B2B features such as company profiles, catalogs, payment terms, quantity rules, and volume pricing. Non-Plus plans are limited to three active B2B catalogs, while Plus supports unlimited catalogs and direct assignment to companies and locations—an important distinction for wholesalers with many pricing arrangements. ([help.shopify.com](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/b2b/catalogs/index?utm_source=openai))

### Choose **Adobe Commerce** if:

- Pricing and catalog rules are unusually complex.
- You operate multiple brands, countries, websites, or business models.
- You need extensive customization of checkout, account structures, or workflows.
- You have internal developers or a capable implementation partner.
- Your ERP, PIM, CRM, or CPQ integration is central to the project.

Adobe Commerce supports shared catalogs, company accounts, B2B quotes, payment and shipping rules, quick order, and requisition lists. Its shared-catalog functionality is specifically designed for custom pricing by company and is suited to businesses managing many catalogs. ([experienceleague.adobe.com](https://experienceleague.adobe.com/en/docs/commerce-admin/b2b/enable-basic-features?utm_source=openai))

## The features I would treat as mandatory

Do not choose based merely on whether the platform can hold thousands of SKUs. Verify that it supports:

1. **Customer-specific catalogs and pricing**
2. **Multiple users per customer account**
3. **Company/location hierarchies**
4. **Price breaks, case packs, minimums, and order increments**
5. **Quick order by SKU and CSV upload**
6. **Reordering and saved lists**
7. **Quotes and sales-rep ordering**
8. **Purchase orders and net payment terms**
9. **Real-time or scheduled ERP inventory synchronization**
10. **PIM integration for product attributes, documents, images, and specifications**
11. **Strong search and filtering**
12. **Tax, freight, and shipping-rule integration**
13. **API/webhook support**
14. **Bulk product and price updates**

## Important architecture advice

For a wholesaler, the ecommerce platform should usually **not** be the primary system of record.

A practical architecture is:

- **ERP:** inventory, customers, credit limits, orders, invoices
- **PIM:** product data, technical specifications, images, documents
- **E-commerce platform:** buyer experience, catalog presentation, cart, checkout, account portal
- **Search engine:** fast SKU, attribute, and faceted search
- **Integration layer:** synchronization between systems

If your ERP already contains customer-specific pricing and inventory, prioritize a platform with a reliable, well-documented integration rather than choosing based on storefront appearance.

## Bottom line

- **Best default:** **BigCommerce B2B Edition**
- **Best for B2B + strong DTC brand:** **Shopify Plus**
- **Best for highly complex enterprise operations:** **Adobe Commerce**
- **Best if you need deeply customized B2B workflows:** **OroCommerce or a custom/headless solution**

For most wholesalers with thousands of products, I would first compare **BigCommerce B2B Edition against Shopify Plus**, then consider Adobe Commerce only if your pricing, catalog, or integration requirements are genuinely complex.

The **best e-commerce platform depends on your budget, technical comfort, product catalog, and growth plans**. For most first-time store owners, I’d shortlist these:

|---|---|---|---|
| **Shopify** | Best overall for most businesses | Easy setup, excellent checkout, strong apps, omnichannel selling, reliable hosting | Monthly fee plus possible app and payment costs |
| **WooCommerce** | Maximum control and flexibility | Open source, highly customizable, no platform transaction fee, works with WordPress | You manage hosting, updates, security, and plugins |

| **Square Online** | Local retailers, restaurants, and service businesses | Free starting plan, excellent Square POS and inventory integration | Less powerful storefront customization and advanced e-commerce features |
| **Squarespace Commerce** | Design-led brands and creators | Beautiful templates, strong content and branding tools | Not as deep as Shopify or WooCommerce for advanced commerce operations |

## My recommendations

### 1. Shopify — best default choice

Choose Shopify if you want to launch quickly without managing servers or technical maintenance. It includes hosting, a full online store, unlimited products, multiple sales channels, and in-person selling. Shopify’s Basic plan is listed at **$39/month monthly or $29/month when billed annually** in the U.S. ([shopify.com](https://www.shopify.com/pricing?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:**  
- First-time entrepreneurs  
- Direct-to-consumer brands  
- Dropshipping and print-on-demand  
- Stores that may eventually sell internationally or in person  

**Watch out for:** paid apps, premium themes, and payment-processing or third-party payment fees.

### 2. WooCommerce — best for flexibility and ownership

WooCommerce is best if you already use WordPress or want complete control over your store’s data, design, checkout, and hosting. The core platform is open source and does not charge a platform transaction fee beyond your payment provider’s fees. ([woocommerce.com](https://woocommerce.com/woocommerce-features/?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:**  
- Content-heavy businesses  
- Custom product requirements  
- Businesses with WordPress expertise  
- Owners who want to choose their own hosting and providers  

**Watch out for:** hosting, security, backups, premium extensions, and developer costs. It can be inexpensive, but it is not necessarily the easiest or cheapest after maintenance is included.

### 3. BigCommerce — best for scaling and complex catalogs

BigCommerce is a strong choice for stores with larger catalogs, multiple sales channels, B2B needs, or more advanced built-in functionality. Its current self-service plans are listed as **Core at $39/month, Growth at $105/month, and Scale at $399/month**, with lower annual-billing prices. It also introduced plan and payment-provider changes beginning **June 1, 2026**, so payment fees and sales-volume thresholds should be checked carefully. ([bigcommerce.com](https://www.bigcommerce.com/pricing/?utm_source=openai))

**Best for:**  
- Established retailers  
- Wholesale and B2B commerce  
- Stores with complex pricing or product structures  
- Businesses trying to reduce dependence on third-party apps  

**Watch out for:** higher starting costs and gross-merchandise-volume thresholds that can move you to a more expensive plan.

### 4. Wix — best for a visually attractive small store

Wix works well when the website and brand presentation are as important as the store itself. It is generally easier for nontechnical users than WooCommerce and gives you substantial control over page design.

**Best for:**  
- Artists, consultants, creators, and boutiques  
- Stores with a relatively small product catalog  
- Businesses combining content, appointments, and commerce  

**Watch out for:** limitations if you later need advanced inventory, international commerce, sophisticated promotions, or highly customized operations.

### 5. Square Online — best for selling both online and locally

Square Online is particularly attractive if you already use Square for point of sale, payments, appointments, or inventory. Its Free plan has no monthly fee; the listed online transaction rate is **2.9% + $0.30**, while paid plans add customization and other features. ([squareup.com](https://squareup.com/us/en/online-store/plans?msockid=1bc36084ea7b6f62259276d6eb156e3d&utm_source=openai))

**Best for:**  
- Restaurants and food businesses  
- Local shops and pop-ups  
- Businesses with physical and online sales  
- Sellers who want simple pickup and delivery options  

**Watch out for:** fewer advanced e-commerce capabilities than Shopify, WooCommerce, or BigCommerce.

## Simple decision guide

- **I want the easiest, safest starting point:** Shopify  
- **I already use WordPress:** WooCommerce  
- **I need B2B, complex products, or serious scale:** BigCommerce  
- **I care most about visual design and simplicity:** Wix or Squarespace  
- **I sell in person and online:** Square Online  
- **I’m testing an idea on a small budget:** Shopify or Square Online  
- **I want full ownership and customization:** WooCommerce  

## Bottom line

For most new online stores, I would choose **Shopify** unless one of these applies:

- Choose **WooCommerce** if you are comfortable with WordPress and want maximum control.
- Choose **BigCommerce** if you expect a complex or rapidly scaling operation.
- Choose **Square Online** if your business is primarily local or already uses Square.
- Choose **Wix or Squarespace** if branding and website design matter more than advanced commerce features.

Before committing, compare the **total cost**, not just the advertised monthly plan: payment processing, apps or extensions, shipping tools, email marketing, domain registration, tax software, and developer or maintenance costs can substantially change the real price.

### 2. Best modern headless option: **Saleor**

Saleor is a strong choice for companies with a capable engineering team building custom web, mobile, retail, or marketplace experiences. It is API-only and GraphQL-native, with support for multi-channel commerce, multiple currencies, languages, warehouses, and extensible apps. ### 3. Best for custom business logic: **Medusa**

Medusa is especially attractive for developers building unusual commerce workflows rather than simply configuring a standard online shop. Its modular architecture includes products, carts, orders, inventory, payments, fulfillment, promotions, regions, and more, while allowing custom workflows, APIs, modules, and admin extensions. **Good fit for:**

- Large product catalogs
- Multiple websites, stores, or currencies
- Complex product configurations
- Wholesale and B2B requirements
- Companies with dedicated developers or an implementation partner

**Avoid it when:** your budget cannot support ongoing specialist development and infrastructure work.

### 5. Best conventional alternative to WooCommerce: **PrestaShop**

PrestaShop is a mature PHP-based open-source platform designed specifically for e-commerce rather than as an extension of a CMS. The project states that it supports internationalization, major payment services, responsive storefront and back-office interfaces, and more than 300,000 stores. ([prestashop-project.org](https://www.prestashop-project.org/about/?utm_source=openai))

**Good fit for:**

For most B2B wholesalers with thousands of SKUs, I’d start with **BigCommerce B2B Edition**.

It offers a strong balance of:

- Customer-specific pricing and catalogs
- Company accounts with multiple buyers and permissions

- Multi-storefront support for separate wholesale, retail, brand, or regional sites
- Less infrastructure management than a self-hosted platform

BigCommerce specifically supports SKU-level price lists, customer groups, bulk ordering, quotes, company hierarchies, buyer permissions, and invoice management. ([bigcommerce.com](https://www.bigcommerce.com/solutions/wholesale-ecommerce-platform/?utm_source=openai))

## Best options by situation

| Situation | Best fit |
|---|---|
| Typical wholesaler/distributor wanting a reliable SaaS platform | **BigCommerce B2B Edition** |
| Very complex pricing, catalogs, workflows, or ERP integration | **Adobe Commerce** |
| B2B-first manufacturer/distributor needing CRM, PIM, workflows, and multi-organization support | **OroCommerce** |
| Strong DTC brand adding wholesale, prioritizing ease of use and speed | **Shopify Plus** |
| Large enterprise with extensive internal development resources | **Adobe Commerce or a composable/headless architecture** |

### 1. BigCommerce B2B Edition — my default recommendation

Choose this if you want to launch relatively quickly without building and maintaining as much custom infrastructure.

It is particularly suitable when you have:

- Hundreds or thousands of wholesale accounts
- Different price lists by customer or customer group
- A mix of retail and wholesale sales
- Multiple brands, markets, or storefronts
- Sales reps who need to place orders for customers
- Customers who reorder using SKUs, CSV files, or saved lists

Its Multi-Storefront functionality can manage separate storefronts with distinct domains, themes, catalogs, customer groups, and price lists from one control panel. ([support.bigcommerce.com](https://support.bigcommerce.com/s/article/Price-Lists?language=en_US&utm_source=openai))

### 2. Adobe Commerce — best for maximum flexibility

Choose Adobe Commerce if your business has unusually complex requirements, such as:

- Many customer-specific catalogs
- Complicated pricing rules
- Parent/child company structures
- Multiple buyer roles and approval chains
- Negotiated quotes
- Purchase-on-account or credit-line purchasing
- Multiple websites, brands, currencies, or regions
- Deep ERP, PIM, CRM, or marketplace integration requirements

Adobe’s B2B tools include company accounts, shared catalogs, custom pricing, quotes, purchase approvals, quick order, requisition lists, and payment on account. Its documentation also describes support for very large catalogs and many prices per SKU. ([experienceleague.adobe.com](https://experienceleague.adobe.com/en/docs/commerce-admin/b2b/shared-catalogs/catalog-shared?utm_source=openai))

The tradeoff is greater implementation complexity, higher development costs, and more ongoing technical ownership than a SaaS platform.

### 3. OroCommerce — best for complex B2B operations

OroCommerce is worth serious consideration if you want a platform designed primarily for distributors, manufacturers, and wholesalers rather than adapting a consumer-commerce platform.

It emphasizes:

- Multiple organizations and websites
- Corporate account hierarchies
- Granular permissions
- Multiple catalogs and price lists
- Warehouse-aware inventory
- RFQs, quick ordering, reordering, and invoicing
- Built-in CRM, PIM, and workflow capabilities

Oro describes its platform as combining B2B ecommerce, CRM, PIM, DAM, invoicing, payments, and workflow tools. ([oroinc.com](https://oroinc.com/b2b-ecommerce/orocommerce-features/?utm_source=openai))

I’d consider it when your sales and operational processes are more complicated than your storefront needs.

### 4. Shopify Plus — best if wholesale is alongside DTC

Shopify Plus is attractive when you already run a successful Shopify retail business and want to add wholesale without introducing a separate platform.

Shopify now provides B2B capabilities on non-Plus plans, including companies, catalogs, payment terms, volume pricing, and quantity rules. However, regular plans have catalog limitations, while Plus supports unlimited B2B catalogs and direct catalog assignment to individual companies or company locations. ([help.shopify.com](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/b2b/getting-started/plan-features?utm_source=openai))

I would choose Shopify Plus when:

- Your DTC operation is already on Shopify
- Your B2B pricing model is relatively manageable
- Brand and marketing experience are very important
- You value operational simplicity
- You do not need extremely complicated quote, approval, or ERP-driven workflows

I would be cautious if every customer has a highly unique assortment and price structure.

## What matters more than the number of products

“Thousands of products” is not, by itself, a reason to choose one platform over another. The critical questions are:

1. **How many unique prices exist per SKU?**
2. **Does each customer see a different product assortment?**
3. **Do customers buy by SKU, spreadsheet, EDI, or punchout?**
4. **Do you need quotes and sales-rep-assisted ordering?**
5. **Are there company hierarchies and approval workflows?**
6. **Where is inventory managed—ERP, WMS, or ecommerce platform?**
7. **Do you need multiple warehouses and real-time availability?**
8. **Will retail and wholesale share one catalog?**
9. **How frequently do products, prices, and inventory update?**
10. **Do you need a PIM for product content and attributes?**

For a large wholesale catalog, I would normally plan for:

- **ERP** as the source of truth for customers, inventory, orders, and financial data
- **PIM** for product descriptions, attributes, images, documents, and category data
- **Ecommerce platform** for browsing, pricing presentation, checkout, account management, and self-service
- **Search layer** with strong SKU, synonym, faceting, and attribute search
- **EDI/punchout integration** if customers use procurement systems

## My practical recommendation

Use this decision rule:

- **Choose BigCommerce B2B Edition** if you want the best general-purpose starting point.
- **Choose Adobe Commerce** if pricing, catalogs, company structures, or integrations are highly complex.
- **Choose OroCommerce** if you want a deeply B2B-oriented operational platform with CRM/workflow capabilities.
- **Choose Shopify Plus** if you are already Shopify-centric and wholesale is an extension of a strong DTC business.

Before signing, require each vendor to demonstrate—not merely promise—the following using your own data:

- Importing your full product catalog
- Searching by SKU, manufacturer part number, UPC, and synonyms
- Customer-specific pricing
- Customer-specific product visibility
- CSV or quick-order purchasing
- Reordering from a prior order
- Quote and approval workflows
- Inventory by warehouse
- ERP price and inventory synchronization
- Performance with your largest customer catalog

For a typical U.S. wholesaler, my shortlist would be **BigCommerce B2B Edition first, Adobe Commerce second, and OroCommerce third**.

#### Best traditional alternative to WooCommerce: **PrestaShop**
PrestaShop is worth considering for a conventional self-hosted store with a sizable product catalog and internationalization needs. The project says it is released under the OSL 3.0 license and supports multiple languages, countries, payment services, and extensive customization. ([prestashop-project.org](https://www.prestashop-project.org/about/?utm_source=openai))

([experienceleague.adobe.com](https://experienceleague.adobe.com/en/docs/commerce-admin/stores-sales/introduction?utm_source=openai))

### Simple decision rule

- **Launching a normal store:** WooCommerce  
- **WordPress already in use:** WooCommerce  
- **Growing B2B or international business:** Shopware

**My default recommendation: migrate to Shopify—Shopify Plus if you have substantial revenue, large traffic spikes, multiple markets, B2B, or complex operations.**

Your two symptoms—**holiday crashes** and **plugin conflicts**—usually indicate that you’re carrying too much infrastructure and third-party code in the critical checkout path. A hosted platform should reduce both risks, though no platform eliminates poorly designed apps or integrations.

### Best fit by situation

| Situation | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| You want the lowest operational burden and reliable peak-season checkout | **Shopify** |
| High-volume store, flash sales, multiple countries/stores, B2B, or advanced automation | **Shopify Plus** |
| You need more native catalog/pricing flexibility and API-driven integrations, but still want SaaS hosting | **BigCommerce Enterprise** |
| Deeply customized B2B, pricing, catalog, or Adobe ecosystem—and you have a strong engineering team | **Adobe Commerce Cloud** |
| Small budget and a team willing to manage hosting, updates, staging, and compatibility | WooCommerce—but it is the least aligned with your stated problems |

Shopify Plus currently advertises unlimited bandwidth, a load-tested checkout handling more than 10,000 checkouts per minute, automatic platform updates, and peak-event infrastructure; those claims should still be validated against your own load profile. ([shopify.com](https://www.shopify.com/plus/pricing?utm_source=openai))

### Why I would not choose another WordPress/WooCommerce setup

WooCommerce’s own documentation acknowledges that themes and plugins increase incompatibility risk and recommends isolating conflicts by disabling plugins one at a time on a staging site. That is useful for troubleshooting, but it is not a fundamental fix for a plugin-heavy production architecture. ([woocommerce.com](https://woocommerce.com/document/how-to-test-for-conflicts/?utm_source=openai))

### Shopify vs. BigCommerce

Choose **Shopify Plus** if:

- Your priority is dependable promotions, checkout, and holiday scaling.
- You want fewer server and update responsibilities.
- Your team prefers vetted apps and managed integrations.
- You sell DTC, retail, internationally, or through multiple storefronts.

Choose **BigCommerce Enterprise** instead if:

- You need unusually flexible product catalogs, price lists, or customer-specific pricing.
- You want more functionality exposed through APIs rather than apps.
- Your current integrations are better supported in BigCommerce.
- You need a SaaS platform but want to avoid relying heavily on storefront plugins. BigCommerce supports app-based integrations, webhooks, channels, and multi-storefront compatibility, but each app still needs to be vetted carefully. ([docs.bigcommerce.com](https://docs.bigcommerce.com/developer/docs/integrations/getting-started?utm_source=openai))

I would choose **Adobe Commerce Cloud** only when customization is a strategic requirement—not simply because the current site is failing. Adobe provides cloud scaling and holiday-readiness guidance, but its own materials still emphasize capacity planning, caching, database optimization, monitoring, and operational preparation. It can be powerful, but it generally requires more technical ownership. ([experienceleague.adobe.com](https://experienceleague.adobe.com/en/docs/commerce/cloud-service/overview?utm_source=openai))

### Recommended migration approach

1. **Inventory every plugin and integration.** Classify each as: replace with native functionality, replace with an app, custom integration, or remove.
2. **Keep checkout integrations minimal.** Avoid stacking multiple scripts for discounts, upsells, tracking, fraud, and payment customization.
3. **Build a staging store and migrate a data copy.**
4. **Load-test realistic holiday scenarios:** concurrent users, inventory contention, coupon launches, bot traffic, payment retries, and order exports.
5. **Run a parallel period** with order, tax, shipping, ERP, email, analytics, and fulfillment reconciliation.
6. **Cut over during a low-volume window**, with rollback DNS and order-processing procedures ready.
7. **Freeze nonessential changes** several weeks before your next major holiday campaign.

**Bottom line:** Unless you have unusual B2B or catalog requirements, I’d shortlist **Shopify Plus first**, **BigCommerce Enterprise second**, and avoid moving from one plugin-dependent WordPress stack to another.

- You have highly complex customer-specific catalogs and price books.
- You need sophisticated approval workflows and quote negotiation.

Do not select based on product count alone. Thousands of products is manageable for most modern platforms. The difficult questions are:

2. **Can one buyer belong to multiple companies or locations?**
3. **Do customers need negotiated quotes or only standard pricing?**
4. **Are there approval rules for purchase orders?**
5. **Do you sell by case, pallet, truckload, or minimum order quantity?**
6. **Can buyers upload CSV orders or enter SKUs quickly?**
7. **How will inventory, pricing, customer credit, tax, and order status sync with the ERP?**
8. **Can sales reps place orders on behalf of customers?**
9. **Do you need punchout procurement, EDI, or marketplace integrations?**
10. **Do you need separate storefronts for brands, regions, or customer segments?**

## Bottom line

- **Best default choice:** **BigCommerce B2B Edition**
- **Best for a DTC-plus-wholesale brand:** **Shopify Plus**
- **Best for deeply customized enterprise commerce:** **Adobe Commerce**
- **Best B2B-native option for complex distributors:** **OroCommerce**

Before signing, require each vendor to demonstrate your real scenarios using sample data: customer-specific pricing, a parent company with multiple locations, a CSV order, an approval workflow, a quote, an ERP price update, and a sales-rep-assisted order. ## What I would avoid

I would **not** respond to this problem by simply moving from one self-hosted plugin stack to another. If you’re currently on WooCommerce, its own documentation acknowledges that theme, plugin, caching, hosting, and “must-use” plugins can all create conflicts. ([woocommerce.com](https://woocommerce.com/document/how-to-test-for-conflicts/?utm_source=openai))

Adobe Commerce/Magento can work for highly customized enterprise businesses, but it generally requires more infrastructure, development, and ongoing performance management—so it may not solve your operational problem unless you have a dedicated engineering team.

## Practical decision

| Situation | Best fit |
|---|---|
| B2C store, holiday spikes, want fewer outages and less maintenance | **Shopify Plus** |
| Complex B2B, catalog, pricing, or API requirements | **BigCommerce Enterprise** |
| Very unusual business model and large engineering organization | Adobe Commerce or composable commerce |
| Smaller store without genuinely enterprise traffic | Standard Shopify or BigCommerce, not necessarily Plus |

### Migration rule

Do not recreate every existing plugin. First classify each plugin as:

1. **Replace with native platform functionality**
2. **Replace with one vetted app/integration**
3. **Build as a small custom extension**
4. **Retire**

Then run a staging load test at least **2–3 times your highest observed holiday traffic**, test payment and inventory concurrency, and keep the old store available during a controlled DNS cutover. Even Shopify advises reviewing third-party integrations before major flash sales because external apps can still fail under increased checkout volume. ([help.shopify.com](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/promoting-marketing/sales/flash-sales?utm_source=openai))

**Bottom line:** choose **Shopify Plus** unless your B2B, catalog, or API requirements strongly favor BigCommerce. The key is not merely changing platforms—it is reducing the number of third-party components in the checkout and promotion path.

For most B2B wholesalers with **thousands of SKUs**, I’d start with **BigCommerce B2B Edition**—unless your ERP or pricing model points strongly toward another platform.

### Recommended shortlist

| Best fit | Platform | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Best general-purpose choice** | **BigCommerce B2B Edition** | Strong wholesale features without requiring a fully custom build: company accounts, buyer roles, price lists, quotes, purchase orders, invoice history, payment terms, bulk ordering, and multi-storefront support. ([support.bigcommerce.com](https://support.bigcommerce.com/s/article/B2B-Edition?language=en_US&r=358&utm_source=openai)) |
| **Best if you already use Microsoft Dynamics or SAP** | **Sana Commerce Cloud** | ERP-centered architecture with real-time product, customer-specific pricing, inventory, order, invoice, tax, and account data. Particularly attractive when the ERP should remain the system of record. ([sana-commerce.com](https://www.sana-commerce.com/solutions/?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Best for highly complex B2B workflows** | **Adobe Commerce** | Deep support for shared catalogs, company-specific pricing, account structures, custom workflows, and extensive APIs. More powerful, but usually more expensive and implementation-intensive. ([experienceleague.adobe.com](https://experienceleague.adobe.com/en/docs/commerce-admin/b2b/shared-catalogs/catalog-shared?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Best if you also have a major DTC brand** | **Shopify Plus** | Excellent operational simplicity, strong storefront performance, and native B2B capabilities such as company profiles, catalogs, volume pricing, payment terms, and headless APIs. Its cost and catalog model need careful evaluation for complex wholesale pricing. ([shopify.com](https://www.shopify.com/plus/pricing?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Best B2B-first platform** | **OroCommerce** | Designed around manufacturers, distributors, and wholesalers, with customer-specific pricing, account hierarchies, multiple catalogs, quoting, and B2B workflows. ([oroinc.com](https://oroinc.com/b2b-ecommerce/orocommerce-features/?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Best for enterprise composable/headless builds** | **commercetools** | Suitable for large catalogs, high transaction volumes, complex pricing, multi-region operations, and custom buyer journeys—but requires a capable engineering and integration team. ([commercetools.com](https://commercetools.com/products/b2b?utm_source=openai)) |

## My practical recommendation

Choose **BigCommerce B2B Edition** if you need:

- Thousands to tens of thousands of products
- Customer-specific price lists
- Company accounts and multiple buyers
- Quick-order by SKU or CSV
- Quotes and sales-rep-assisted ordering
- Purchase orders and payment terms
- Reordering and saved shopping lists
- A SaaS platform rather than a heavily managed custom system

It is generally the strongest **balance of B2B functionality, implementation speed, and maintainability** for a mid-market wholesaler. That is my recommendation based on fit—not a claim that it is universally the best platform.

Choose **Sana** instead if your pricing, inventory, customer credit, availability, and order rules already live in **Dynamics 365, NAV, AX, SAP Business One, or SAP S/4HANA**. In that case, avoiding duplicated business logic may matter more than storefront flexibility. ([support.sana-commerce.com](https://support.sana-commerce.com/Content/Sana-User-Guide/System/ERP-Connection.htm?utm_source=openai))

Choose **Adobe Commerce or OroCommerce** if you have complicated account hierarchies, negotiated pricing by customer and SKU, multiple business models, sophisticated quoting, or unusual ordering workflows.

Choose **Shopify Plus** if the business is primarily a brand-led DTC operation adding relatively straightforward wholesale—not if wholesale is the core operating model with many unique customer contracts.

## Don’t choose based on SKU count alone

“Thousands of products” is usually manageable for all of these platforms. The more important questions are:

1. **How many unique price lists are there?**
2. Are prices negotiated at the **customer, customer group, product, or SKU** level?
3. Do customers need **quotes, approvals, purchase orders, or credit limits**?
4. Is real-time inventory required across multiple warehouses?
5. Which system owns products, pricing, inventory, tax, customers, and orders?
6. Do buyers need **CSV ordering, EDI, PunchOut, or procurement integrations**?
7. Do you need one storefront, multiple brands, or regional sites?
8. Do you need both B2B and DTC from the same platform?

### Bottom line

- **Default recommendation:** BigCommerce B2B Edition  
- **ERP-driven wholesaler:** Sana Commerce Cloud  
- **Complex enterprise B2B:** Adobe Commerce or OroCommerce  
- **DTC-first company with simpler wholesale:** Shopify Plus  
- **Large engineering organization building a custom commerce stack:** commercetools  

Before selecting one, run a proof of concept using real data: **10,000 representative SKUs, several actual customer price lists, inventory by warehouse, a quote, a PO order, and a reorder workflow**. That will reveal more than a feature checklist.

- **BigCommerce:** $39/month for Core, $105 for Growth, and $399 for Scale when billed monthly; annual billing reduces those to $29, $79, and $299 respectively. Its Performance plan starts around $1,499/month billed annually. ([bigcommerce.com](https://www.bigcommerce.com/pricing/?utm_source=openai))

### Costs beyond the subscription

You should also allow for:

- **Payment processing:** commonly around **2.5%–3.5% plus a fixed fee per order**. For example, Shopify lists standard online card rates starting at 2.9% + $0.30, while Squarespace lists rates starting at 2.5% + $0.30. ([shopify.com](https://www.shopify.com/pricing?utm_source=openai))

- **Premium theme or design:** optional; can be a one-time cost or a recurring service expense.
